blocks.content: Handling disagreements covered the most common, lowest stakes form of friction, disagreeing on a specific decision. Conflict with teammates goes further, into situations where the friction is not just about one decision anymore, it has become genuine tension in the working relationship itself.

This distinction matters because the two require different handling. A disagreement usually resolves once a decision gets made. A real conflict with a teammate can linger well past any single decision, quietly affecting every future interaction until it is actually addressed.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022337948-426858739.png
blocks.alt: Conflict with teammates moves from disagreeing on a decision to genuine, lingering friction in the working relationship itself

blocks.content: 1. Disagreement Versus Genuine Conflict

It helps to be precise about the difference. A disagreement is different views on one specific decision, and it usually resolves once that decision gets made, even if you did not get your preferred outcome. A genuine conflict is friction in the working relationship itself, and it can linger, coloring every future interaction, long after the original decision is settled.
Recognizing which one you are actually in matters, because a genuine conflict needs more than just resolving the original decision, it needs the relationship itself to be actively repaired.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022340152-889983107.png
blocks.alt: A disagreement usually resolves once the decision is made; a genuine conflict can linger in the relationship well past that decision

2. Common Root Causes

Peer conflict rarely comes out of nowhere. A few real root causes show up repeatedly, unclear ownership over the same piece of work, leading to stepped on toes and duplicated effort. A past incident that was never actually addressed, quietly accumulating resentment. Mismatched expectations about pace or quality, where one person feels the other is moving too fast or too slow, or cutting corners.

Naming the actual root cause, rather than a vague sense of just not getting along, is what makes a conflict resolvable at all. Most peer conflicts that never get resolved stay stuck specifically because nobody named the real underlying cause.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022341850-710615543.png
blocks.alt: Common root causes of peer conflict include unclear ownership, unaddressed past incidents, and mismatched pace or quality expectations

blocks.content: 3. A Worked Example

A concrete story shows what resolving real peer conflict looks like. Ongoing tension had built up with a peer over overlapping ownership of the same module, leading to friction in nearly every interaction between them.

First person quote: "I had ongoing tension with a peer over overlapping ownership of the same module, we kept stepping on each other work without meaning to. Instead of letting it keep building, I initiated a direct, private conversation. I named the specific friction clearly, the overlapping ownership, rather than making a vague complaint about our working relationship in general. We agreed on clear boundaries for who owned what going forward, and the tension genuinely eased once we both had that clarity."
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022343500-599316574.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: initiating a direct conversation, naming the specific friction, and agreeing on clear ownership boundaries going forward

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Naming the conflict only as a vague feeling, we just do not work well together, rather than the specific, addressable root cause underneath it. A vague complaint is much harder to actually resolve than a specific one.
4. Avoiding the Conflict Versus Addressing It
blocks.text: 4. Avoiding the Conflict Versus Addressing It

blocks.content: Avoiding the person, or avoiding the topic entirely, feels easier in the moment, but the friction usually grows rather than shrinks over time, since the underlying issue never actually gets resolved, it just gets buried under more accumulated resentment.

Addressing it directly and early, even though it feels uncomfortable, usually resolves faster than expected, precisely because the issue gets named and dealt with before it has time to compound into something bigger and harder to untangle.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022345106-990859725.png
blocks.alt: Avoiding a peer conflict usually lets the friction grow over time; addressing it directly and early usually resolves it faster than expected

blocks.content: 5. Repairing Trust After a Real Conflict
blocks.text: 5. Repairing Trust After a Real Conflict

blocks.content: Resolving the immediate issue is not always the same as fully repairing the relationship. A few things genuinely help rebuild trust afterward, following through consistently on whatever was actually agreed, since broken follow through undoes the resolution quickly. Not bringing the old conflict back up unnecessarily once it has been resolved. And giving the relationship genuine time to rebuild, rather than expecting it to feel completely normal again immediately.

This is worth naming in an interview answer too, since a story that ends the moment the immediate conflict is resolved, with no mention of the relationship afterward, is less complete than one that shows the relationship was actually repaired over time.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022346707-810057243.png
blocks.alt: Repairing trust after a real conflict takes consistent follow through, not reopening the old issue unnecessarily, and genuine time

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A resolved conflict and a repaired relationship are not automatically the same thing. The relationship repair often takes real, deliberate follow through well after the original conversation.
6. Genuinely Common Failure Modes

A few real patterns undermine how people handle peer conflict. Letting resentment build silently instead of addressing it, until it eventually surfaces in a much less controlled way. Involving the whole team in what is really a two person issue, which can make the conflict feel bigger and more public than it needs to be. Addressing the conflict in the moment but never actually repairing the relationship afterward, leaving lingering awkwardness.

A strong interview answer often names one of these honestly as something learned through experience, which shows real growth in handling peer conflict rather than a claim of having always gotten it right.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022348278-323775455.png
blocks.alt: Common failure modes: letting resentment build silently, involving the whole team unnecessarily, and never repairing the relationship afterward

blocks.content: 7. Choosing Your Own Conflict With Teammates Story
blocks.text: 7. Choosing Your Own Conflict With Teammates Story

blocks.content: Look for a genuine conflict, not just a disagreement, where the relationship itself was actually affected, and where you took a deliberate step to address it directly rather than letting it linger or escalating it unnecessarily.

The strongest stories here show both halves clearly, addressing the immediate issue and actively repairing the relationship afterward, since a story that only covers one half feels incomplete to an interviewer listening closely.
Resolving the issue and repairing the relationship are two different steps, and both matter.

items: Making the story mostly about the other person flaws: the interviewer is evaluating your handling of the conflict, not judging the other person.
Skipping straight to escalation without a direct conversation first: reads as conflict avoidant, even if escalation was eventually appropriate.
Ending the story without mentioning the relationship afterward: leaves out the part that usually matters most, whether trust was actually rebuilt.
